messages.content: You write dialogue that reveals character through voice and rhythm.
Write a dialogue between a detective and a suspect during interrogation. The detective bluffs about having evidence. The suspect is innocent but acts guilty out of fear.

message.content:
# The Interview Room

---

The fluorescent light above the table flickered once, twice, then held steady. Detective Mara Vance set a manila folder on the metal surface between them and let it sit there, unopened.

"Thirty-seven years," she said. "That's how long I've been doing this job. You know what I've learned in that time?"

The suspect—Daniel Marsh, twenty-eight, junior accountant—shook his head too quickly.

"I've learned that everyone in this chair thinks they're smarter than me." She tilted her head. "They're always wrong."

"I haven't done anything, I keep telling you—"

"Daniel." She said his name like a parent correcting a child. "I haven't said what you haven't done."

Silence. The folder sat between them like a loaded gun.

"We have the security footage from the Whitmore building," Mara said. It was a lie. "We have your fingerprints on the server room door. We have the access logs that show you were there at 2:47 AM on Tuesday night."

Daniel's hand moved to his collar, tugging it loose. "That's—that's not possible. I wasn't—"

"You weren't there?"

"I wasn't—" He stopped. Swallowed. "Look, I can explain. If you'd just let me—"

"I'm letting you talk right now."

"But you're not *listening*."

Mara leaned back in her chair. She didn't blink.

Daniel's knee bounced under the table. "I drove past the building. That's all. I drove past it. I didn't go *in*. I don't even have a keycard, I don't have clearance, I—"

"Yet your prints are on the door."

"Then someone—" He stopped again. His eyes darted to the folder, then away. "Someone planted them. That's what you're going to say, right? That's what guilty people say?"

"Guilty people say a lot of things."

"Innocent people say a lot of things too!"

The words came out too loud. Daniel flinched at the sound of his own voice.

Mara didn't flinch. She just watched.

"I'm sorry," he whispered. "I'm sorry, I just—I don't understand why I'm here. I don't understand any of this. I have a job, I have a girlfriend, I pay my taxes, I—"

"Daniel."

"—I'm not a *criminal*, I don't even speed, I—"

"*Daniel.*"

He stopped. His hands were shaking now. He pressed them flat against his thighs.

Mara opened the folder. She looked down at a blank page, then closed it again.
